title: AI in Dutch business · from idea to report

idea.title: The idea
idea.text:
**How is AI changing Dutch businesses, and what does it mean for a bank such as ABN AMRO?**

The starting point for an Insights-style article for business readers. Nothing is decided yet: where to look, which numbers to trust, what to test.

agent.title: Research AI in Dutch business
agent.text:
Research how AI is changing Dutch businesses, for a bank's business clients. Six directions and eight web searches: official Dutch figures, Europe for comparison, small businesses, what a bank already says, rules for small firms, and whether AI pays off.

*Recorded for this demo on 11 October 2026, outside ros.ai. In a live run Claude Code makes this plan here, and nothing is searched until you approve it.*

directions.result: CBS's AI monitor is the primary source. In 2024, 22.7% of Dutch companies with ten or more workers used at least one AI technology, nearly 9 points more than in 2023 [3]. Use was highest among companies with 500 or more workers (59.2%) and lowest among those with 10 to 19 (17.8%) [3]. Five EU countries had a higher share than the Netherlands; the EU as a whole stood at 13.5% [3]. The monitor counts seven specific technologies, such as machine learning and text mining [2], and its second chapter gives the figures by company size, with each group's share of turnover [1]. DutchNews reports the same CBS figures [4].

directions.result: Two sources reach below ten employees. A CBS report on micro businesses, summarised by MKB Servicedesk, finds that almost 14% of Dutch micro businesses used AI technologies in 2025 [1]. A survey of more than 1,700 entrepreneurs for Exact's MKB Barometer puts use at 70% in 2026, up from 33% in 2025 [2]. They measure different things: CBS asks about specific technologies, the survey asks whether entrepreneurs use AI at all. The other results are a company press release and statistics round-ups [3][4][5].

directions.result: ABN AMRO's June 2026 Insights article finds that 78% of organisations with turnover up to €25 million use AI to some degree, but only 9% have a formal policy for outside AI tools, and that smaller firms are the least prepared for new digital risks [1]. A 2023 article on 73 retailers finds just over half already working with AI, with most saying their in-house knowledge falls short or will be a challenge [4]. Two results cover the same 2026 research [2][3]; one is about the bank's own use of AI, not its clients [5].

L40: Publication date: 18/06/2025 06:30 Dutch AI monitor 2024
L41: # 2 .Use of AI technology by Dutch companies
L42: 
L43: This chapter examines the use of AI technologies by Dutch companies with ten or more employees.
L44: 
L45: Questions on use of AI technology in survey on ICT use in enterprises
L46: The data used for this chapter were taken from the cite34†survey on ICT usage in enterprises. This survey describes ICT use among firms with at least one person employed in sections C through N and Q of the NACE classification of economic activities. Since 2020, it has included a series of questions about the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which are posed to companies with ten or more employees.
L47: They ask whether companies use specific AI technologies, for what purposes these AI technologies are used, and how the AI technologies were obtained. Companies indicating that they do not use AI are asked if they have ever considered using such technology, and if not, for what reason. There is some variation over the years in the questions asked, as well as the response categories used. A summary of these questions and categories can be found in cite30†Appendix 1 .
L48: For the period 2021-2024, the use of at least one of the following seven AI technologies could be identified consistently: machine learning, service robots or autonomous vehicles, robot-assisted process automation, speech recognition, image recognition, text mining and natural language generation. However, a consistent time series from 2020 onwards could only be established for the first four of the listed technologies.
L49: cite35†Eurostat†ec.europa.eu defines the investigated technologies as follows.

L244: ## 2.2 Revenue share of companies with AI technology
L245: Companies that used AI technology accounted for more than half (51.1 percent) of the total turnover in 2024 by companies with ten or more employees in sectors C through N and Q; companies that did not use AI accounted for the remaining 48.9 percent of turnover. The revenue share of companies that used AI technology was greater among larger companies.
L246: For example, among companies with ten to nineteen employees, those that used AI technology accounted for 18.7 percent of turnover, compared with 79.5 percent for companies with 500 or more employees. This positive relationship between revenue share and company size can be partly explained by the fact that larger companies are more likely to use AI technology.

pages.title: CBS · Increasing use of AI by business
pages.text:
Excerpts of this page as read on 11 October 2026. Each passage is word for word; text between passages is left out.

Published 27 February 2025.

In 2024, 22.7 percent of companies with ten or more workers used one or more forms of AI technology.

This was an increase of nearly 9 percentage points compared with 2023.

This is according to CBS’s AI Monitor 2024.

Larger companies were more likely to use AI technology in 2024 than smaller companies.

Use of AI technology was the most common among companies with 500 or more workers (59.2 percent)

and the lowest among companies with 10 to 19 workers (17.8 percent).

In 2024, there were five EU countries (Denmark, Sweden, Belgium, Finland, and Luxembourg)

with a higher share of companies that use AI technology than the Netherlands.

Across the European Union as a whole, 13.5 percent of companies used AI technology in 2024.

pages.title: CBS · Dutch AI monitor 2024, summary
pages.text:
Excerpts of this page as read on 11 October 2026. Each passage is word for word; text between passages is left out.

In 2024, 23 percent of companies with ten or more employees made use of one or more of the AI technologies listed.

The seven technologies are: machine learning, service robots or autonomous vehicles, robot-assisted process automation, speech recognition, image recognition, text mining and natural language generation.

Among those companies which, in 2024, had considered adopting AI technology at some point, but which were not currently using it, ‘lack of experience’ was by far the most commonly given reason for this (75 percent).

pages.title: BIS Working Paper 1325 · AI adoption, productivity and employment: evidence from European firms
pages.text:
Excerpts of this page as read on 11 October 2026. Each passage is word for word; text between passages is left out.

23 January 2026.

Our results show that AI adoption increases the level of labor productivity by 4%.

Productivity gains are due to capital deepening, as we find no adverse effects on firm-level employment.

However, productivity benefits of AI adoption are unevenly distributed and concentrate in medium and large firms.

pages.title: VoxEU · How AI is affecting productivity and jobs in Europe
pages.text:
Excerpts of this page as read on 11 October 2026. Each passage is word for word; text between passages is left out.

Inaki Aldasoro, Leonardo Gambacorta, Rozália Pál, Debora Revoltella, Christoph Weiss, Marcin Wolski, 17 February 2026.

AI adoption increases labour productivity levels by 4% on average in the EU

we find no evidence that AI reduces employment in the short run

The productivity benefits, however, are unevenly distributed.

medium and large companies experience substantially stronger productivity gains than their smaller counterparts

The capital-deepening effects we document may be transitional.

findings.claim: Larger Dutch firms use AI more often
findings.quote: Larger companies were more likely to use AI technology in 2024 than smaller companies.
findings.why: The size gap is the core of the story; the next step tests it on CBS's own table.

findings.claim: The same size gap across the EU
findings.quote: In 2025, 17% of small enterprises, 30.36% of medium enterprises and 55.03% of large enterprises used AI.
findings.why: The Dutch pattern is not unusual: AI use rises with size across Europe.

findings.claim: Productivity gains go to bigger firms
findings.quote: However, productivity benefits of AI adoption are unevenly distributed and concentrate in medium and large firms.
findings.why: If gains follow size, the adoption gap can widen differences between firms.

findings.claim: 22.7% of firms with ten or more workers use AI
findings.quote: In 2024, 22.7 percent of companies with ten or more workers used one or more forms of AI technology.
findings.why: The official baseline, counting seven specific AI technologies.

findings.claim: Almost 14% of micro businesses use AI
findings.quote: Bijna 14% van de Nederlandse microbedrijven gebruikte in 2025 AI-technologieën.
findings.why: Covers the firms CBS's main monitor leaves out, with the same kind of technology list.

findings.quote: Zeven op de tien ondernemers (70%) zeggen de technologie inmiddels te gebruiken, tegenover een derde (33%) in 2025.
findings.why: Asking whether a firm uses AI at all gives a far higher number than asking about specific technologies.

findings.claim: 78% of SMEs use AI to some degree
findings.quote: Tegelijk gebruikt 78 procent van deze organisaties – met een jaaromzet tot 25 miljoen euro – in enige mate AI
findings.why: A second any-use measure, from the bank's own research.

findings.why: Readiness falls with size, as use does.

findings.quote: ‘lack of experience’ was by far the most commonly given reason for this (75 percent).
findings.why: Among firms that considered AI but did not use it, the barrier is know-how.

themes.title: AI use rises with company size
themes.description: Official Dutch and EU figures agree: the bigger the firm, the more likely it uses AI, and the productivity gains follow the same line.

themes.title: How you ask changes the number
themes.description: Counting specific AI technologies gives 14–23%; asking whether a firm uses AI at all gives 70–78%. An article must say which measure it uses.

themes.title: Use runs ahead of readiness
themes.description: Few firms have rules for AI tools, smaller firms are the least prepared, and lack of experience is the main barrier.

aside.reason: 73 retailers in 2023: too narrow and too old for a national picture.
About support for firms that build AI; the question is about use.

conclusion.title: Leading conclusion
conclusion.text:
**AI use in Dutch business rises steeply with company size, and readiness lags behind use.**

- **Size:** 22.7% of Dutch companies with ten or more workers used AI in 2024, from 17.8% of the smallest to 59.2% of the largest. The EU shows the same gradient: 17% of small and 55% of large enterprises in 2025.
- **Measure:** CBS counts specific AI technologies. Surveys that count any use report 70–78%, so the measure must be named.
- **Readiness:** only 9% of SMEs have a formal policy for outside AI tools, and productivity gains so far concentrate in medium and large firms.

**Next:** test the size gap on CBS's own table, and check what the turnover shares do and do not say.
